newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rubber-Thais creating two-tier market, trade quiet.
newsitem.headline: Rubber-Thais creating two-tier market, trade quiet.

text.p: Thailand may be digging itself a hole by engaging in a rubber buying spree to prop up the market, especially if prices head south as expected in the coming weeks, traders said on Monday.

A senior Thai Agriculture Ministry official said last week the government had bought some 26,400 tonnes of RSS3 rubber since March 5 and intends to buy more, Rubber dealers in Singapore estimate Bangkok has already purchased more than 30,000 tonnes.
"The Thais are creating a two-tier market and storing up trouble for themselves," one senior rubber dealer said.
"Why should anybody pay them 126 (U.S. cents a kg) in a 118 (cents) market?" the dealer added.

The Thais have been buying RSS3 rubber at 123.50 cents a kg and have dominated activity in Southeast Asian markets over the past few weeks. Dealers in the city-state said Bangkok is hoping to sell the rubber at 125.00-126.00 cents.
"The (Thai) government intervention helped but the impact of such a move would be limited until the real buying picks up," a Thai trader said.
"This is really political. The Thais want to hold the prices up for the smallholder. If the prices don't go up, they're in trouble," a dealer in Singapore said.

The Thai market expects the government will be able to secure some rubber deals with China when Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh visits Beijing this week. A Thai commerce ministry official said on Monday Thailand had targeted sales of 400,000 tonnes of rubber to China this year.
But a trader with a Japanese rubber dealing house in Singapore was sceptical the Thai government would find buyers for all the rubber it had bought.
"They may be able to sell a part of it to China in some barter deals, but consumer demand is really flat. Who's going to buy all that rubber?" the dealer said.
"The amount China can buy is limited," a Singaporean rubber trader added.

The Thai benchmark RSS3 rubber for May delivery was quoted around 121.00-122.00 US cents a kg FOB Bangkok compared with 123.00 cents on Wednesday. Concentrated latex was quoted around 92.00 cents a kg from 93.00 cents last week.
Southeast Asian rubber prices may dip further this week due to soft consumer demand, traders said.
"We expect the price to move in a narrow range this week with a downward bias unless there are new leads in the market," a Thai trader said.

"Prices have not recovered yet. I think things will get worse in the coming days because buyers are taking advantage of the current low prices by asking for July/August shipment," said an Indonesian trader.

A Singapore dealer said prices will probably drift lower with the wintering period, when rubber trees shed their leaves and latex flow slows, almost over and a supply glut seen in the May/July period.
"You may see a serious decline in prices," one said.
"Usually, wintering will cause tight supply and this would automatically boost prices. But it is not happening now," an Indonesian trader said.
Indonesian dealers said U.S. customers had already piled up sufficient stocks.
They said a deal was done at 50.75 U.S. cents a lb for July shipment FOB Medan and offer prices were quoted at 50.50 cents for May/June shipment.
Offer prices were quoted at 50.50 cents FOB Surabaya and Palembang, at 50.25 cents FOB Padang and at 50.00 cents FOB Pontianak and Jambi -- all for May/June shipment.
"This situation will keep prices down. In addition, demand is very poor," an Indonesian dealer said.
Malaysian rubber prices, on the other hand, will continue moving in a tight band.

The Malaysian Rubber Exchange and Licensing Board (MRELB) quoted the benchmark RSS1 rubber at Malaysian 298.50 cents a kg and the SMR20 at 285 cents a kg, both for April buyer, at the close of the market last week.
"Whichever way it goes, I don't see it falling or rising by more than one or two cents," said one trader in Malaysia.
The RSS1 could test the 300 cent-level and the SMR20 the 287-level this week if demand improves, but buying in the market remains weak.

Some Malaysian rubber suppliers were hopeful that European demand will return to the market strongly after the current Easter holiday period. "But I doubt it," a trader said. "There's no indication that they (the Europeans) are short of supply."
Despite the wintering season, dealers reported there were ample supplies of latex, which was trading at 234 Malaysian cents a kg last week.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
